title: Comprehensions
intro: A **comprehension** builds a list in one line from a loop: `[n * n for n in range(5)]`. Add `if` at the end to keep only some items. The same shape builds sets `{…}` and dictionaries `{key: value for …}`.

questions.prompt: Read it as *make this, for each item, if this is true*.
questions.exampleCode:
squares = [n * n for n in range(5)]
evens = [n for n in range(10) if n % 2 == 0]
lengths = {w: len(w) for w in ["hi", "hello"]}
letters = {c for c in "banana"}
print(squares)
print(evens)
print(lengths)
print(sorted(letters))
questions.explanation: A comprehension replaces *create empty list, loop, append*.

questions.prompt: Store each price in `prices` with 20% tax added, rounded to 2 decimals, in `with_tax`. Use a list comprehension.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert with_tax == [round(p * 1.2, 2) for p in prices], 'with_tax should be each price × 1.2, rounded to 2 places.'

questions.explanation: The expression on the left is applied to every item.
Comprehensions work over any sequence, including strings.

questions.prompt: Store the temperatures above 20 from `temps` in `warm_days`, keeping their order.
questions.solution: warm_days = [t for t in temps if t > 20]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert warm_days == [t for t in temps if t > 20], 'warm_days should keep only temperatures above 20.'

questions.hint: Put the condition at the end: `… for t in temps if …`.
questions.explanation: The `if` filters; the left part says what to keep.

questions.prompt: What does `{x % 3 for x in range(10)}` produce?
questions.hint: Curly brackets with single values make a set.
questions.explanation: The remainders repeat, but a set keeps each once.

questions.prompt: This should list the length of each word, but it raises a *NameError*. Fix it.

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert lengths == [len(w) for w in words], 'lengths should be the length of each word.'

questions.hint: The loop variable must match the name used on the left.
questions.explanation: `for word in words` names each item `word`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the value so `lengths` maps each name to its length.
questions.template:
names = ["Ana", "Bo", "Cleo"]
lengths = {name: ___ for name in names}

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert lengths == {'Ana': 3, 'Bo': 2, 'Cleo': 4}, 'lengths should map each name to its length.'

questions.hint: What goes after the colon is the value.

questions.prompt: `emails` is a list of addresses. Store the **different** domains (the part after `@`) as a sorted list in `domains`. Build a set comprehension first.
questions.solution: domains = sorted({e.split("@")[1] for e in emails})

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert domains == sorted({e.split('@')[1] for e in emails}), 'domains should be the distinct parts after @, sorted.'

questions.hint: `e.split("@")[1]` is the domain. A set comprehension removes repeats.

questions.code: print([n for n in range(10) if n % 4 == 0])

questions.prompt: `products` is a list of `(name, price, in_stock)` tuples. Build a dictionary `available` mapping name → price, for items that are in stock **and** cost under 50. Use a dict comprehension.
questions.solution: available = {name: price for name, price, in_stock in products if in_stock and price < 50}
questions.setupCode: products = [("mug", 8.5, True), ("lamp", 45.0, False), ("chair", 79.0, True), ("rug", 39.9, True), ("vase", 12.0, False)]

tests.name: value
tests.code: assert available == {n: p for n, p, s in products if s and p < 50}, 'available should include only in-stock items under 50.'

questions.hint: Unpack the three values in the `for` part, then filter with `if … and …`.
questions.explanation: Unpacking, filtering and building a dict — all in one readable line.
